Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we all know AI can get expensive.
  • Also: Microsoft states its fresh AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
  • In a recent development, earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft states its fresh AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

In a recent development, earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

In a recent development, if it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s big bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions.

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:.

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Industry observers note that software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

According to recent reports, instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

Then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s latest.

According to recent reports, what comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

There’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically claims, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”.

Sources indicate that in other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving manufacturer labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the company saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your company needs a chief AI officer in 2026.

Sources indicate that I find it particularly telling that this is from the company that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

Sources indicate that that’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

In a recent development, microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the firm’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the firm’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:.

It has been revealed that this means the company doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

Leading scale, lowest gas prices, and heavy daily traffic: Home to over 1,800 locations across the Southeast and Midwest portions of the U.S., Murphy is the fourth-largest convenience-store chain in the country. Thanks to a now-defunct partnership with Walmart (WMT +1.51%), most of Murphy's locations are next to some of the mega-retailer's stores, drawing heavy daily shopping traffic from customers typically focused on finding the best deals.

Massive share buybacks: Powered by its outsize pump traffic, Murphy not only sells tons of gas at a slim profit, but also ample high-margin inside merchandise (snacks, beverages, nicotine, etc.). While the dividend currently yields only 0.54%, it pairs well with the company's buybacks, as the company can increase payments if the stock ever trades at a higher valuation.

Everything Is Falling Apart, and AI’s Fingerprints Are All Over It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.
  • But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto.
  • In a recent development, something must be behind all of this, you might think—a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have struggled to find the time to write this story about why everything keeps breaking because everything keeps breaking.

Microsoft Outlook? Broken, for a bit. Air traffic control? Had some challenges. Bank with Chase? Monday was not great. But even before that, you had issues if you ran a website with PHP, or had a grocery store freezer connected to the internet, or owned crypto. I am almost certainly forgetting some.

In a recent development, something must be behind all of this, you might think—a massive cyberattack campaign, maybe or AI agents running amok across the internet? But the answer is more complicated than that. All of these problems, and the ones that will happen after I write this, are probably unconnected, at least in the concrete sense. But they exist in a world where the infrastructure of the internet and the whole human world it undergirds looks increasingly precarious.

Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counter adversary operations at cybersecurity tech giant CrowdStrike, called last month “Black October.” This month? “Blacker November.” December probably isn’t looking great.

“This is not getting better, unfortunately,” Meyers told me.

One big reason for all of this, although not the only one, is artificial intelligence, but maybe not in the ways you expect.

It has been revealed that if it’s connected to the internet, it’s at risk. Websites, sure. But also utilities like power plants and water treatment facilities or, for some reason, grocery store freezers.

In the olden days, like six months ago, a hacker taking control would have required a fairly complicated set of skills, honed over a long career, perhaps in the employ of a government or criminal organization.

In a recent development, artificial intelligence, especially models developed and released this year, has changed things. AI has “democratized” hacking, cybersecurity experts told me. Things that used to require the capabilities and focus of a team of people with a clear goal can be done by a 20-something with an AI model and a specially designed program around it. And you don’t have to be a big or valuable target anymore to be worthy of a hacker’s attention.

It has been revealed that at the same time, AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities. These models and agents — essentially AI models that can do things on their own — can comb through websites or code and find problems that might have escaped the notice of humans. And they can do so more cheaply, meaning they can be turned on code that might not otherwise have gotten a close look. So many vulnerabilities are being exposed that it’s been given an appropriately bleak name: the vulnpocalypse.

Even that defensive advantage is a double-edged sword. Before, it might have taken weeks before a newly discovered vulnerability could be exploited. Now it might take days, even hours. If you’re responsible for a website or any of those things connected to the internet that may or may not still be maintained by their creators, you may not be paying attention and know you should enhancement. You may find yourself liable if a breach leads to a leak of customer data. You may not have the know-how to fix it.

It has been revealed that another risk introduced by AI is that the technology, trained on all the lines of code its creators could find, is really good at writing code. Software engineers know this, and companies are now maintaining smaller teams of human engineers using AI to write more and more software. That code might be OK, but it might not be, and there’s a chance no human ever looked at it to be sure.

According to recent reports, when I connected with John Strand over video chat, he was in Germany for a conference, and he was smiling. That wasn’t good. “You need to understand that whenever an offensive security person smiles and gets excited,” he said, “it’s bad.”.

As owner and CEO of Black Hills Information Security, Strand’s job is to test systems for weaknesses, to think like an attacker and poke holes in a client’s defenses. He says he’d been getting a bit bored with the work after decades of the same techniques until the cyber capabilities of AI models started to explode at the end of 2025. Fresh AI models were great at finding weaknesses in code, and AI agents could do the boring, time-consuming part.

“You’re seeing something that can automate the kind of grinding grunt work of offensive security and bring that to a human operator much faster,” Strand said.

Industry observers note that things have only accelerated since the summer. AI agents are capable of more autonomy. And attackers have better tools to refine the often blunt instruments of AI models — harnesses. While an AI model can do a lot of things, a harness provides the tools and direction that allow it to do a specific thing more effectively. Think Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI’s Codex, but for hacking. Perhaps the biggest, most notable harness used by hackers is Artex, a significant-enough threat that the FBI issued a warning last week.

Sources indicate that in September and October, a hack of major South Korean banks led to the theft of personal information. Meyers says CrowdStrike determined the attacker was likely a 26-year-old in China using Artex. After asking AI how to do the attack, the hacker succeeded, then asked the AI how to sell the stolen data on Telegram.

“Anybody out there can now be a nation-state-level hacker just by using the tool,” Meyers remarked.

Despite efforts by major AI developers to limit who can access their biggest and most capable models, the hacking and exploit skills attackers need are within the means of models already in the hands of attackers. That includes open-weight models that hackers can run on their own hardware, away from the guardrails and peering eyes of AI companies and government agencies.

“The genie’s out of the bottle, and there’s no putting it back in,” mentioned Gary Barlet, public sector chief technology officer at Illumio, a firm that specializes in ransomware and breach containment.

In a recent development, AI-powered hackers, whether they’re individual vibe-hackers or government-backed cyberwarfare units intent on damaging critical infrastructure, always have an advantage. They just have to be right once, as the saying goes. Defenders have to be right every time.

The good thing is that the defenders are using the same tools as the attackers. And sometimes they have a head start. Programs like Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, OpenAI’s Daybreak and Google’s Fairwind let cybersecurity experts and high-profile targets like banks and healthcare providers have early access to the most capable models from those developers, often with fewer limits on what the models can find. The goal is to get a jump on patching and fixing the easiest and riskiest problems.

Sources indicate that it still might not be enough, and Big Tech leaders know it. In an October appearance at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he no longer thought we’d be able to “just patch all the bugs” and that the problem is one that “is still something that we have not, as organizational leaders or countries or individuals, taken seriously.”.

Industry observers note that and defenders may not have much of a lead in patching bugs anyway, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week at the New York Times Dealbook Summit. Previously, when patching a critical system, you might have a week to test it before pushing it to production. “Right now the patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild,” Nadella said. “That’s going to create instability.”.

The PHP vulnerability widely reported in October — with an urgent notice from the PHP Foundation for website owners to patch — stemmed from work through Patch the Planet, part of OpenAI’s Daybreak.

Recent findings suggest that that’s just one high-profile recent disclosure. But there has been an avalanche of them. The National Vulnerability Database has received more than 10,000 instances of common vulnerabilities and exposures so far in November, after more than 17,000 CVEs in October. For comparison, in October 2025, that figure was less than 5,000.

“There’s effectively this big backlog of security issues in the open-source world that hadn’t been discovered until AI was able to just spend tons of time analyzing it and finding these vulnerabilities,” remarked Matt Wyckhouse, CEO of Finite State, a cybersecurity company focused on connected devices.

It goes well beyond open-source software. The connected devices Wyckhouse focuses on include things like refrigerators and smart home gadgets — the kinds of things that probably didn’t have to be connected to the internet, but are. The source code of the firmware and software powering those products has been seen by far fewer eyes than something like PHP, an incredibly common coding language used by much of the internet. The code running these devices may not be on GitHub or floating around the internet, but an AI model might be able to reverse-engineer it and find an exploit. And suddenly an attacker can turn freezers into ovens. If you think ground beef is expensive now, imagine what would happen if a major retailer’s stock of hamburger all spoiled overnight.

“Refrigeration has to work for our society to function, as it turns out,” Wyckhouse said.

Wherever the vulnerability is found, it has to be patched. That’s where the backlog of issues is really wreaking havoc. Companies that create or just operate software are swamped with key, critical issues that have to be fixed now because it could only be hours before an attacker can exploit it. It’s why your computer and the software on it have to update so frequently these days.

“It’s daunting the amount of work and the amount of time it’s going to take to clean this whole thing up,” mentioned Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov.

Industry observers note that and patching isn’t perfect. Sometimes it’s not a cyberattack that causes a system to go down but the fix to prevent it. Software updates are believed to be responsible for several of the recent high-profile outages, including Apple’s challenges on Tuesday.

Things get even hairier if the code isn’t great to begin with or presents fresh problems of its own. And with AI writing even more of it, that’s a growing glitch.

Sources indicate that in the backdrop of all of this chaos is the fact that software engineering is one of the industries most disrupted by AI. Models trained on miles of code are great at writing something that works — no matter how many holes are in it. And to CEOs eager to cut costs and boost their companies’ stock prices, the temptation is to lay off engineers and have fewer people use AI to do all that coding.

In a recent development, significant Tech has been laying off staff by the thousands this year. Microsoft’s October announcement that it was offering buyouts to 60,000 staff became a key talking point just weeks later when the system powering its Outlook email service went dark for a day. Might things break less often if more people were on hand to maintain them?

“I wouldn’t be surprised if companies start to backtrack on that more,” said Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing at the database security firm Liquibase.

Companies might also have more junior developers writing and releasing code that would have previously gone through senior developers, with AI replacing the productivity, but not the experience, McCurdy says.

In a recent development, that means the problem isn’t just the vulnerabilities in existing software, but the vulnerabilities being written into fresh software or patches to existing software by AI. The same technology is causing the problem, providing the solution and complicating that solution.

The main thing we can do now is just… wait. Wyckhouse told me he thinks the next two years are going to be a period of growing pains as vulnerabilities are found and patched. The end result should be that everything is more stable.

It has been revealed that “I think software is going to be an order of magnitude more secure by the end of the next year or two than it is today for this reason,” he said. “It will hurt a bit.”.

Whether you’re an ordinary phone user or a major corporation, updating your software has become more vital than ever.

Industry observers note that “You’ve got to patch. You go for a flu shot, and you go and have your preventative healthcare,” Meyers said. “You need to do the same thing when it comes to cybersecurity.”.

Sources indicate that but consumers aren’t without power, especially when it comes to data breaches. If a firm isn’t properly maintaining its systems and protecting your privacy or security online, don’t use it. Having your data hacked and compromised has become ordinary. We get letters in the mail saying someone stole data from our bank or doctor’s office, and if we jump through the following hoops, we can get 12 months of identity protection.

We don’t have to put up with it, Barlet claims. “I think we need to start having higher expectations from the companies we’re consuming from,” he said.

I can't believe everyone missed the 'Derry Girls' creator's hilarious Netflix murder mystery

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Too many murder mysteries telegraph their twists a mile away.
  • It premiered quietly on Netflix back in February, earned glowing reviews, and then more or less vanished, skipped by audiences and passed over for a second season despite being one of the smartest things the streamer put out all year.
  • If you’re ready for a wickedly funny mystery that’ll have you laughing one minute and gut-punched the next, keep reading.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Too many murder mysteries telegraph their twists a mile away. This scrappy little series takes a familiar setup and pushes it somewhere much weirder and funnier than you’d expect. Three women in their late 30s reunite for the funeral of a childhood friend, only to start suspecting her death was no accident. That’s how “How to Get to Heaven from Belfast” opens — and it might just be the funniest, most underrated show most people never bothered to watch this year.

It premiered quietly on Netflix back in February, earned glowing reviews, and then more or less vanished, skipped by audiences and passed over for a second season despite being one of the smartest things the streamer put out all year. The show comes from Lisa McGee, the creator of the beloved “Derry Girls,” though you shouldn't walk in expecting more Catholic-schoolgirl hijinks. This is a darker, twistier beast: a genuine murder mystery that happens to be laugh-out-loud funny, trading teenage chaos for middle-aged mayhem. Across eight tightly wound episodes, McGee’s razor-sharp writing and a trio of electric lead performances turn a simple whodunit into a story about grief, friendship, and the secrets we bury—all set to a killer ’90s soundtrack.

If you’re ready for a wickedly funny mystery that’ll have you laughing one minute and gut-punched the next, keep reading.

In a recent development, saoirse (Roisin Gallagher), Robyn (Sinéad Keenan), and Dara (Caoilfhionn Dunne) were inseparable as teenagers in Belfast, part of a tight-knit group of four. Now in their late 30s, they’ve drifted apart and moved on with their lives — until the sudden death of the fourth member of their group, Greta, brings them back together for her funeral.

What should be a simple reunion swiftly spirals into something a lot weirder. The women start to suspect that Greta’s death wasn’t the accident everyone’s calling it. In fact, it may tie directly to a secret from their shared past, one they’ve spent years trying to forget.

Determined to find out what really happened, the trio releases an investigation that takes them well beyond Belfast — even landing them at a resort in Portugal — as the past they’ve been outrunning finally catches up with them.

According to recent reports, I’ll keep this simple: The show is funny, the mystery is sharp and the two actually work in tandem. Most of the credit goes to Lisa McGee’s writing. She pulled off the same balancing act on “Derry Girls,” where the comedy never undercut the emotional gut-punches. Doing it again here with older characters and darker stakes makes the show feel far more grounded than most mysteries in its lane.

Industry observers note that roisin Gallagher, Sinéad Keenan, and Caoilfhionn Dunne play women who’ve known each other since childhood, and you buy it immediately. They bicker, cover for each other, and slip back into old habits the way real lifelong friends do. Their chemistry is electric—and given how much time they spent together on set, it’s easy to believe that bond carried over off-camera.

Best of all, it’s a self-contained eight-episode miniseries, meaning the whole story is here and it actually has an ending—no cliffhangers. You can knock it out in a weekend without worrying about Netflix abruptly pulling the plug on a resolution.

It didn’t get nearly the attention it deserved the first time around, which is exactly why it’s worth seeking out now. If you want a smart, funny mystery you can start and finish without a massive commitment, it’s streaming on Netflix — so make sure to catch it (and “Derry Girls” too, if you haven't already).

Stream "How to Get to Heaven from Belfast" on Netflix.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption.
  • During the keynote for the manufacturer’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella revealed Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.
  • Also: Microsoft states its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring.

During the keynote for the manufacturer’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella revealed Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.

Also: Microsoft states its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several newly introduced Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets, which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework.

“As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft said. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.”.

Microsoft also announced Autopilot, a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described.

In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots, but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft mentioned, and assign it tasks.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s new Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector.

Microsoft said the agent will be able to autonomously handle “meetings and follow-ups on its own,” though that claim may be best verified by teams themselves.

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

According to recent reports, “Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft said.

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

Nadella also revealed a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. Right now in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up quickly,” Microsoft said of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill.

In a recent development, microsoft also revealed that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can rapidly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft unveiled a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

According to recent reports, agent 365, which Microsoft announced last year, is the company’s observability platform. Microsoft noted Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft showed how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

“It starts with a new way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft stated. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”.

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

Sources indicate that “Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft noted. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise looks.

ULA Vulcan Launch Ends in Disaster for Amazon's Satellite Internet Ambitions

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for months, Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -7.69%) CEO Elon Musk had been making noises about ending commercial releases of its Falcon 9 rocket -- the rocket that, in 2025, rolled out more than 80% of all payloads to orbit worldwide.
  • It has been revealed that nine months ago, United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered an anomaly with one of its Vulcan Centaur rockets, forcing it to pause operations while it worked out a fix.
  • A successful launch would advance Amazon's effort to build a satellite communications system to rival SpaceX's Starlink.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Rich Smith – Nov 21, 2026 at 9:27PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Amazon ›.

A crisis was forming in the space industry.

According to recent reports, for months, Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -7.69%) CEO Elon Musk had been making noises about ending commercial releases of its Falcon 9 rocket -- the rocket that, in 2025, rolled out more than 80% of all payloads to orbit worldwide. At the time, rockets from rival companies Arianespace, Blue Origin, and United Launch Alliance were all grounded for a variety of technical glitches.

It has been revealed that nine months ago, United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered an anomaly with one of its Vulcan Centaur rockets, forcing it to pause operations while it worked out a fix. But at long last, ULA was ready to return to flight. In a mission slated for Nov. 15, Vulcan would return to flight, carrying a payload of 40 Leo communications satellites into orbit for customer Amazon (AMZN -4.10%).

A successful launch would advance Amazon's effort to build a satellite communications system to rival SpaceX's Starlink. At the same time, it would alleviate the concerns of space companies worried that Falcon 9's retirement would deprive them of access to space. With ULA back in the race, there'd once again be an alternative to SpaceX.

That's what a successful launch would have meant -- but it's not what actually happened.

Instead, for the first time in its history as a space tech giant, ULA suffered a total mission failure -- all cargo lost. As ULA explained, its Vulcan rocket "lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight," although the real problem occurred before that.

Vulcan Centaur includes two stages: BE-4 engines from Blue Origin power the Vulcan first stage, supplemented by RL10 side boosters from L3Harris(LHX -2.59%). In flight, the RL10s are first to drop off the rocket, followed by the entire first stage detaching approximately six minutes into flight. Then the Centaur second stage takes over and lifts the payload the rest of the way into orbit.

According to recent reports, after several days of examining the data, ULA now believes the RL10 boosters and the second-stage Centaur both performed nominally. The problem must therefore lie with the Vulcan first stage -- specifically, preliminary indications as of Wednesday suggest Vulcan's fuel supply to the BE-4 engines, rather than the engines themselves, was the culprit. This first stage performed poorly in the boost stage, failing to accelerate the vehicle sufficiently for the Centaur to lift the payload all the way into orbit.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

For Amazon, either culprit would be bad news.

Aiming to accelerate its deployment of Leo satellites so that it can begin competing with SpaceX in satellite internet, Amazon splashed out billions of dollars to reserve launches on 38 Vulcan Centaur rockets, 18 Arianespace Ariane 6es, and anywhere from 12 to 27 Blue Origin Fresh Glenns.

It's also reserved introduces on some of ULA's older Atlas V rockets. So far, those have done most of the work of putting nearly 400 Amazon Leo satellites into orbit (with significant help from SpaceX's Falcon 9, which Amazon reluctantly added to the lineup in 2023). The problem is, ULA is just about out of Atlas V rockets (and isn't building more). And SpaceX Falcon 9 launches are all booked up through 2028 (and SpaceX also doesn't plan to add more).

This leaves Amazon largely dependent on ULA's Vulcan Centaur -- which just proved itself unreliable. And this problem may get even bigger; after all, the same BE-4 engine that appears to be at the root of Vulcan's problems also powers Blue Origin's Upcoming Glenn rocket. And that could put New Glenn on the sidelines as well.

If that's the case, then Blue Origin's Latest Glenn may not be affected.).

Still, until this is all resolved, it appears that Amazon currently has no reliable means of putting Leo satellites into orbit.

#108242. Breaking: One Month and a Half-Million-Plus Folds Later, Our Machine Is Still Testing the iPhone Duo

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1105 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: One Month and a Half-Million-Plus Folds Later, Our Machine Is Still Testing the iPhone Duo

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo folding phone came out a month ago.
  • How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo?
  • I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo folding phone came out a month ago. Every day since then, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, a dedicated machine inside CNET’s lab has been folding and unfolding it over and over again. For science.

How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of Friday, Nov. 20, we’re up to more than 565,000 folds and the Duo hasn’t broken yet. The hinge has shown signs of potential failure, however. Our technicians, as well as the cameras and sensors that are part of our testing rig, continue to monitor the situation and collect data.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. My team and I designed and built this proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

My team of engineers and testing experts has been watching the iPhone Duo open and close, over and over, for the past few weeks to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review as well as her one-month-later follow-up. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a newly introduced-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

Sources indicate that in many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.).

Industry observers note that moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

It has been revealed that we determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

According to recent reports, we also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

Sources indicate that to secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

Industry observers note that there’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

According to recent reports, apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

#108239. Expert reveals 7 common bedroom items that can trigger 3 a.m. wake ups — here’s what to remove from your bedroom to start sleeping through the night

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2102 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomsguide ↗ Open Full Page

Expert reveals 7 common bedroom items that can trigger 3 a.m. wake ups — here’s what to remove from your bedroom to start sleeping through the night

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2102 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here at Tom's Guide, we know that nighttime wake-ups are a big matter for many people.
  • You might not realize it, but elements of your sleep space could be contributing to your disrupted rest — from technology and light usage, to elements of your bed itself.
  • With advice from two sleep experts, we're exploring why bedroom environment matters, what to consider changing and why those adjustments are notable for sleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here at Tom's Guide, we know that nighttime wake-ups are a big matter for many people. Which is why, if you've found yourself repeatedly awake at 3 a.m. and unable to fall back to sleep, it's time to take a look around your bedroom.

You might not realize it, but elements of your sleep space could be contributing to your disrupted rest — from technology and light usage, to elements of your bed itself. The simple act of removing them might be the difference between another broken night's rest and staying asleep all night.

With advice from two sleep experts, we're exploring why bedroom environment matters, what to consider changing and why those adjustments are notable for sleep.

Temperature, light and sound pollution can all stop you from staying asleep all night."People sleep better when it's dark, when it's quiet, when it's cool, when it's free of disturbances [and] when it's safe, claims Dr. Aric Prather, sleep scientist and expert at UCSF and BetterSleep. "And so, trying to optimize that environment on those facets, is certainly a step towards a better night of sleep.".

According to recent reports, while 3 a.m. wake ups have a variety of causes, there are environmental factors that can contribute to them happening, and keep you awake. Here, we explain what they are, and how removing certain items from your room can help.

Both experts we spoke to advised, where possible, to keep work outside of the bedroom. And since many of us work on computers or laptops at home, removing these from your sleep space can help eliminate distracting light sources and potential stress they're associated with.

The Sleep Foundation points out that having electronics near the bed can contribute to nighttime wakeups through the noise and light they can emit. So, we asked Heather Darwall-Smith, a UKCP psychotherapist specializing in sleep and author of The Science of Sleep, if laptops in the bedroom can be impactful on sleep, through the association with work or light from charging cables.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Sources indicate that if it's your work laptop and it's near your bed and you see the light [this can prompt], 'Oh, that's my work laptop. Oh, God, did I send that email?'.

"It's both," she indicates. "The mind needs to know the day is done. It's like putting work away. It's creating that boundary between work and home," she explains.

Industry observers note that dr. Prather also points out that waking and seeing a light from a laptop charging cable can carry anxiety. "Because if it's your work laptop and it's near your bed and you see the light [this can prompt], 'Oh, that's my work laptop. Oh, God, did I send that email?'" he says, adding that it can also lead to ruminating over the next day being a work day.

It has been revealed that he adds that "some people's computers have fans that are constantly running and there's heat coming out of them. So that can change the the temperature of the room or the temperature near their body.".

As temperatures drop over the winter, keeping your heating on overnight can appear to be a sensible way to combat the seasonal chill — but being mindful of temperature is key to avoiding waking up.

Recent findings suggest that “High temperatures in your bedroom can interfere with your body’s natural cooling process, which is essential for falling and staying asleep,” Dr. Hannah Patel previously explained.

Industry observers note that but turning your heating off in the lead-up to bedtime — ideally anytime from around 9 p.m. (though that's not a hard and fast rule if you're an early bird or a night owl!) — you'll allow your bedroom time to cool down.

Similarly, sleeping with an electric blanket is another nighttime practice to be particularly careful with.

Not only is it unsafe to keep an electric blanket on all night (the Electrical Safety Foundation International states they should never be used while sleeping), even modern models with built-in protection to prevent overheating, advise turning off before falling asleep.

Removing your phone from the bedroom is something the Tom's Guide sleep team swears by, in part because expert advice suggests that scrolling your phone late at night can cause a state of mental arousal that may lead to disrupted sleep.

According to recent reports, not to mention, a recent study found that every hour spent on screens before bedtime increases the risk of insomnia by a whopping 59%. As Dr. Prather points out, "phones on their own aren't really problematic, but if people can't keep their hands off them, then they are.".

And while the jury is still out on how much blue light from screens is really going to affect your sleep, looking through your phone in the middle of the night can stimulate your brain and prolong awakenings.

However, Darwall-Smith notes that she often finds "people are more stressed by taking the phone out of the bedroom than having it there.".

If that's you, consider "turning off your notifications, thinking about how checking the screen or getting into live activity on your phone is going to keep you awake," the sleep psychotherapist advises.

It's the literal foundation of your sleep, but you might not have considered that your mattress could be playing a substantial part in disrupting it.

Waking up with back pain or stiffness, aching shoulders and hips, overheating during the night, tossing and turning, and even waking up coughing and sneezing can all be signs that your mattress is the culprit behind your nighttime wake ups.

According to recent reports, "If you're constantly having back pain or your mattress isn't okay... look into it," says Darwall-Smith, though she points out that back pain might be caused by factors outside of your mattress.

Dr. Prather suggests finding a mattress that is "the right comfort for you, and that probably changes as you age," and recommends "one that supports your posture [and] that doesn't cause pain.".

However, as Darwall-Smith notes, "sometimes it's not in [people's] control to change their mattress. So what can you do to make the mattress comfortable? You might want a topper." The best mattress toppers can adjust the comfort and feel of your mattress, and even help with regulating the temperature, all without the cost involved in replacing your existing bed.

Having the wrong pillow for your sleep position, one that has lost it's shape and support, is aggravating allergies or is causing neck pain can all contribute to nighttime wakeups.

Recent findings suggest that research shows a relationship between an uncomfortable pillow and poor sleep. One study looking at pillow performance found that everyone "who reported poor sleep quality also reported poor pillow comfort.".

Sheets, meanwhile, might be something of an afterthought, but synthetic fabrics can trap heat and cause sweaty wake-ups — even though the often low price-point can seem attractive.

In a recent development, dr. Prather notes that along with the right mattress, "the quality of the sheets," and their "breathability" as well as "the quality of the pillow, can all contribute to how comfortable people are, and certainly comfort is something that we want to foster when we're trying to get people to sleep well.".

Our best pillows of 2026 can help you determine what's right for you and our guide to the best bed sheets sets of the year has options for different sleep preferences, seasons, and budgets.

While a basic alarm clock can be a better option that relying on your phone, if it's visible from your bed it's potentially making nighttime wakeups worse.

"I prefer people to use actual alarm clocks and to try and find non-alarming alarm clocks," indicates Darwall-Smith. However, she adds that "I prefer people not to look at their clock.".

According to research, clock-watching or 'time monitoring behaviour' (TMB) is common in people who experience insomnia, and something that perpetuates the symptoms of the condition.

Looking at the clock when you wake during the night is "only bad news" states Dr. Prather. "I deal with people with insomnia, but most people are looking at the clock hoping that it's later in the night than it is. And they're almost always wrong.".

Being aware that it's not as late as you hoped then leads to "an immediate anxiety or frustration or discouragement, which pushes against falling back asleep," he explains.

Obviously, we're not suggesting getting rid of the main light in your bedroom altogether, and living each evening in a state of complete darkness.

Sources indicate that but if you find yourself awake during the night? "You should not turn on big lights," notes Dr. Prather. "If you can keep it low light, that's certainly better.".

Speaking of light at night, Darwall-Smith explains that "if you're shining light into your brain at 4 a.m., that's not [good]. Because sleep is reset by the light-dark cycle. As we push towards wakefulness, our eyes register light and it's part of what pushes us up into [being] awake.".

However, Dr. Prather cautions against "[sitting] in the dark with your thoughts, usually that isn't a good solution." He recommends activities that are sleep supportive, relaxing and distracting, like reading with a book light, or using a Kindle on low intensity.

Being wide awake in the middle of the night is rarely pleasant, but you don't always have to be concerned by a brief awakening.

"Waking up during the night is normal... it's part of sleep structure. Especially as people get older, it would be very uncommon for people to not wake up during the middle of the night," says Dr. Prather.

Perfectionism is insomnia's best friend.

Sources indicate that darwall-Smith agrees, adding that, "What we're looking at is the quality of what that waking is. If you get up, wander around, go and have a pee, go back to bed, happy days. You get up and your eyes are peeled to the ceiling and you're freaking out, not so happy days.".

Industry observers note that and though we've covered ways you can help your sleep by adjusting your bedroom environment, the experts we spoke to emphasized focusing on what works for you, and not adding stress by focusing on creating a 'perfect' environment. "We're not looking for perfection. We're looking for good enough to sleep better," says Dr. Prather.

It has been revealed that darwall-Smith agrees: "Perfectionism is insomnia's best friend. And if we're rushing around trying to perfect our sleeping conditions, Well, do we really need to? Good enough is good enough.".

According to recent reports, we've talked about what to remove, but there are useful products which can help tackle complications with noise, light and comfort that may be impacting your night's rest. You don't need to strive for absolute perfection, consider these as tools for a calmer, more relaxing night. Even better, these three items are all reduced in the Black Friday mattress deals.

Google Gemini Partners With Watch Duty to Clear Static From Firefighter Radio

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (469 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on Friday, Google’s Gemini team unveiled the results of a upcoming partnership with the wildfire-tracking app Watch Duty, after Gemini engineers spent six months embedded with Watch Duty’s first responders.
  • The Gemini AI improvements got a real-world test during Washington state’s Railroad Fire in July 2026, when Watch Duty issued what it calls its first-ever nighttime Critical Alert.
  • According to recent reports, “This is something the tool also has the capability to do if reports of flooding are communicated via radio,” said Dave Merritt, co-founder and chief technology officer of Watch Duty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on Friday, Google’s Gemini team unveiled the results of a upcoming partnership with the wildfire-tracking app Watch Duty, after Gemini engineers spent six months embedded with Watch Duty’s first responders. The results cut vital new wildfire dispatch translations down to seconds and helped improve radio communications, which can be rough on the front lines of a new fire.

The Gemini AI improvements got a real-world test during Washington state’s Railroad Fire in July 2026, when Watch Duty issued what it calls its first-ever nighttime Critical Alert. The alert stemmed from a nearly unintelligible, static-filled 911 call that the Gemini tool transcribed in under 30 seconds. That kind of assistance can help Watch Duty send alerts to affected communities more swiftly and enable first responders to update maps more accurately and make better-informed decisions.

According to recent reports, “This is something the tool also has the capability to do if reports of flooding are communicated via radio,” said Dave Merritt, co-founder and chief technology officer of Watch Duty. “Across disasters, we hear feedback every day that first responders are using Watch Duty for additional situational awareness, especially for disasters that span multiple counties.”.

Watch Duty reporters are active and retired first responders who can manually monitor up to 20 different feeds, though static and rapid-fire jargon can make them difficult to follow.

Gemini workers used more than 20,000 hours of Watch Duty radio recordings to train the AI tool to recognize firefighting terms that aren’t in the average dictionary or books that AIs are typically trained on.

Google says the tool is not designed to replace human decision-making in life-or-death situations.

“This tool takes on the demanding work of listening, freeing Watch Duty’s volunteers to focus on what matters most: confirming fires and getting warnings to people while they can still act,” stated Stephanie Chew, Google project team lead.

The project was completed at no cost thanks to a Google.org fellowship, and the resulting Watch Duty app features are free to use.

From the data collected, Gemini engineers and Watch Duty identified several measures of success.

According to recent reports, one metric was the word error rate, which fell by around 15% after the AI model was implemented. Another sign of success was a jump in Watch Duty volunteers’ satisfaction with their radio transcription tools, from around 35% to 92%.

The Gemini tool continues to analyze approximately 200 hours of radio speech traffic from 400 feeds per day. The tool was made to handle more than 10,000 radio feeds if necessary.

It has been revealed that MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

According to recent reports, the approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft noted it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman noted during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

Sources indicate that the dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the company has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Industry observers note that western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026.

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman stated of the new coding model the company declared at Ignite.

In a recent development, the firm also released its latest image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

Industry News: I tested the iPhone 18 Pro Max vs Xiaomi 18 Pro Max in a 11-round camera shootout — here is the winner

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The iPhone 18 Pro Max isn't the only 18 Pro Max to be released this year, now that Xiaomi has just revealed the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max flagships.
  • Recent findings suggest that the iPhone 18 Pro Max is one of the best camera phones, sporting a trio of 48MP camera lenses: one main, with variable aperture, an ultrawide angle, and a telephoto lens with 4x optical zoom.
  • You'd think that the higher resolution camera would produce the best photos, right?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The iPhone 18 Pro Max isn't the only 18 Pro Max to be released this year, now that Xiaomi has just revealed the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max flagships. The two phones share more than just a name, though, and it seems Xiaomi has adopted a very Apple-looking camera bump on the back of its phones. But considering the camera specs are totally different, I started wondering what the actual quality differences were.

Recent findings suggest that the iPhone 18 Pro Max is one of the best camera phones, sporting a trio of 48MP camera lenses: one main, with variable aperture, an ultrawide angle, and a telephoto lens with 4x optical zoom. The zooming camera offers up to 16x "optical quality" and has a maximum magnification of 40x. The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, on the other hand, has a 200MP main lens, a 50MP ultrawide and a 200MP telephoto with 3.2x optical zoom.

You'd think that the higher resolution camera would produce the best photos, right? Well we've seen time and again that resolution doesn't always equal quality, especially now that camera phones rely on software just as much as they do hardware. That's why phones like the iPhone 18 Pro Max perform so well in our photo shootouts.

According to recent reports, but obviously the only way to find out for sure is to actually take some photos and compare the results from each phone. So, out of iPhone 18 Pro Max and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which 18 Pro Max actually has the best cameras?

The latest and best iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro Max comes with a new variable aperture camera, a larger battery, incredible performance from the A20 Pro chipset and all those other things that make the iPhone worth owning.

While not officially available in the U.S., the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max has a lot of great features. They include a rear-mounted display, 200MP main and telephoto camera lenses, a 6.98-inch display with Privacy Display and an enormous 7,050 mAh battery.

It has been revealed that the main camera shot is quite different on both phones. The Xiaomi certainly excels in taking a brighter photo, but the result means that the lighter areas look considerably more washed out compared to the iPhone. The overall quality isn't as good either, since the iPhone can pick up more detail in the surroundings, such as my dogs' fur and the gravel on the path. In contrast, the Xiaomi tends to blur those finer details together, especially in the background.

According to recent reports, shooting indoors, things are a little more balanced, but it's clear that the Xiaomi's camera isn't quite as focused as the iPhone's, and most of the Lego set is blurry in comparison to Apple's camera. However the coloring and detail seem to be much closer than they were with the outdoor shot.

The Xiaomi camera's habit of brightening up the image seems to work in its favor on the ultrawide angle lens, with the iPhone adopting a more washed out and drab-looking color temperature. There are reasons for that, and it all comes down to Apple's automatic white balance being somewhat anti-Fall.

Recent findings suggest that however, coloring aside, the detail on the iPhone-captured shot just isn't there. You can even see it in the grass if you look closely, with all the stalks looking pixelated and blurred, compared to the much sharper detail captured by the Xiaomi.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to color, the Xiaomi does edge the top spot with slightly more vivid coloring of these berries, in part thanks to the slightly brighter images. The iPhone hasn't washed out the coloring in this instance, and manages to offer a nice bright image with solid contrast between the different colors.

Sources indicate that the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's front camera sports a 50MP sensor, compared to the 18MP one on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, but how much of a difference does it make? As was the case with the rear cameras, the photo is a lot brighter, which really highlights the fact that the sun is shining directly onto my face. Meanwhile the iPhone's shot is a little darker, but the tones seem more true to life and don't make it look like this is my first time outside in several months.

In a recent development, the quality is good on both, even going so far as to pick up the reflection of my other dog in my sunglasses. However, zooming in indicates how much of a difference high resolution can make. Xiaomi's rendition of my reflected dog is clear and almost perfect, while the iPhone's is pixelated and grainy. Then again, the rest of the photo is fine, and zooming right in isn't something a lot of folks will be doing.

According to recent reports, xiaomi's Portrait mode is, honestly, incredibly disappointing. The bokeh effect is barely noticeable, and it doesn't really emphasize myself in the same way that the iPhone does. The IPhone 18 Pro Max ramped up that effect to the point where the background isn't that visible, and it makes me pop out a little more. The quality of the photo isn't quite as good, but with the extra bokeh and the return more accurate coloring, it's the clear winner.

Zooming into 4x magnification and things are fairly even. The iPhone's coloring is a little more drab than Xiaomi's, but the overall quality of the zoomed-in shot is basically the same, to the point where it's more about personal preference than anything else.

Jumping up to 8x magnification and you can see how Apple's "optical quality" feature really shines. The shot of my dog at this magnification is much more clear than that of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, which noticeably merges the finer details of my dog's fur. The contrasting colors on the Xiaomi's telephoto is more noticeable than the iPhone's, but the loss of quality really lets the team down.

Recent findings suggest that if you increase the magnification to 40x, there's absolutely no question about which camera is better. It's Xiaomi's, simply because the phone produced a clear and crisp shot that the iPhone just can't compete with. I assume some AI upscaling was involved, as is the case with so many other phones, and it's something that Apple consistently fails at. Maybe that's something Apple can include on the iPhone 20.

In a recent development, going right in with the Macro mode, and the iPhone takes the crown once again. As with before, the picture isn't as bright as Xiaomi's shot, but that doesn't actually matter in this case. The iPhone managed to produce a much crisper photo, with bright colors and details that Xiaomi's camera didn't quite match.

Low light performance can make or break a camera phone, and I'm honestly a little torn over which camera is better in this situation. The iPhone 18 Pro Max produced a shot that is brighter and captured more detail, but it also appears somewhat overexposed in the process.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max managed to capture less detail on the church and its surroundings, despite the higher resolution camera, but produced a shot that looks slightly nicer — so long as you don't zoom in too much. And, honestly, I can't tell you which one I like better.

According to recent reports, overall, the iPhone 18 Pro Max managed to beat out the Xiaomi in more categories, though, the two phones drew in several rounds. That demonstrates that Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's camera is no slouch, but not enough to beat the iPhone's camera in those core categories. The quality of the 8x zoom in particular was especially disappointing, since a 200MP lens should have the resolution to be able to cut down a high-quality image to simulate extra magnification — just like Apple does.

Given the choice, and purely based on camera performance, I'd pick the iPhone 18 Pro Max over the Xiaomi. Still the iPhone 18 Pro Max didn't dominate, and the Xiaomi camera certainly manages to produce some great shots. The fact they tied in four different categories just goes to show that these two phones are both very capable camera phones.

But Xiaomi obviously needs to work on fixing its shortcomings, including capturing more detail in low light, improving the bokeh effect and all those other things that could make the camera even better.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that look, we weren’t all lucky enough to lock in PTO for the release of Grand Theft Auto 6. Not everyone gets to write a review of the most anticipated video game in recent memory, or live blog their first 24 hours roaming around Vice City.

In a recent development, A lot of folks are still working away, daydreaming about getting back on the sticks and knocking off corner stores as Jason and Lucia right now. Some people are even on work trips or vacations away from their home consoles right now – let’s keep them in our thoughts.

But even if you find yourself away from home, that doesn’t mean you’re completely locked out of playing GTA 6. Sure, the game may currently be console-locked to the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S, but there are still clever ways to get the game booted up when you’re on the go.

Here’s everything you need to know about the remote play features that you’ll need to take this modern Bonnie and Clyde story on the road.

So long as you have a PS5 or an Xbox with GTA 6 downloaded and ready to go, you can experience the game through smaller devices even when you’re away from home.

Both modern consoles support remote play, a feature that lets you stream your game from your home setup.

If you’re looking to turn on the Xbox’s remote play feature, you need to access the Profile & System settings in the Xbox guide. From there, you need to navigate to the Devices & Connections menu and choose the Remote features option.

Sources indicate that you’ll need to enable the remote features and put your console into sleep mode in order to pair your chosen remote play device. Remote play devices include smartphones, tablets and Windows computers.

Recent findings suggest that gamers who own a PlayStation 5 will need to follow similar steps to get remote play functioning on a mobile device. Within the PlayStation’s settings menu, navigate to the System tab and choose Remote Play. Toggle the Enable Remote Play option. From there, all of the necessary device pairing and gameplay setup will happen through the PS Remote Play app, which you can download on your handheld device.

It has been revealed that whether you own a PlayStation or an Xbox, you’ll want to ensure your console settings are tuned so it stays connected to the internet in rest mode. You’ll also need to enable the console to turn on via a network connection. These settings will allow you to start a remote play session anytime, even if you’ve already left your home.

Sources indicate that if you’re using PlayStation’s remote play feature, you don’t have to fiddle around with gaming tablets or third-party handheld devices in order to find a comfortable way to play GTA 6. Sony’s PlayStation Portal is the perfect console accessory for natural gameplay, since it retains the DualShock controller design.

In a recent development, GTA 6 isn’t coming out on PC for a while still. That limits how many options you have when it comes to taking the game on the go with you. If (for whatever reason) you don’t have access to any remote play options, that leaves you with only the most inconvenient and unwieldy way to take the latest crime simulator with you on the road.

You’ll have to lug around your PS5 or Xbox wherever you go to get in some GTA time – but hey, at least the gaming industry’s deteriorating respect for physical media means you won’t have to keep track of a disc.

The PS5 Slim is probably the easiest current-gen console to carry with you, since the digital edition weighs less than 6 pounds. But you’re giving up the best possible performance available on the PS5 Pro.

Either way, you’ll be carrying around a large, expensive piece of hardware, so this option should only be considered if you really can’t get remote play functioning for whatever reason.

It has been revealed that microsoft’s video game ecosystem is huge, with Game Pass and streaming options available for PC players. But the Xbox brand isn’t offering gamers a cheat code to play GTA 6 on their beefy rigs (or any convenient handheld devices).

Sources indicate that GTA 6 is only available on Xbox consoles with Xbox Cloud Gaming at this time. The upside is that this option lets you play the boundary-pushing new game on the Xbox One, which is very close to being two console generations old.

At that point, you’re better off biting the bullet on a current-generation console and considering the available remote play options.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›.
  • Industry observers note that david Tepper of Appaloosa Management is considered one of the world's top hedge fund managers, and through his investment prowess, he's amassed an estimated net worth of $28.5 billion.
  • While Tepper's track record speaks for itself, I think he got it wrong in this case.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 21, 2026 at 10:00PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›.

Industry observers note that david Tepper of Appaloosa Management is considered one of the world's top hedge fund managers, and through his investment prowess, he's amassed an estimated net worth of $28.5 billion. The Carolina Panthers' owner was reshuffling his artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor positions in Q3, exiting positions in Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -13.25%) and Broadcom (AVGO -12.19%), while buying shares of Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) and Micron (MU -13.89%). He also cut his stake in Alphabet (GOOGL -2.70%) (GOOG -2.59%) nearly in half.

While Tepper's track record speaks for itself, I think he got it wrong in this case. Here's why.

It has been revealed that while Tepper was buying Nvidia shares before Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO, the company is facing potential problems beyond the loss of its CEO. Competitors have started to catch up, with Semianalysis recently reporting that Alphabet's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), which it co-developed with Broadcom, are delivering better performance per dollar. Meanwhile, all of Nvidia's largest customers, outside of Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -7.69%) are working on developing their own custom chips.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

It has been revealed that the AI application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) market is growing much more rapidly than the GPU market, with Counterpoint Research projecting that custom AI chip unit shipments will surpass data center GPU shipments in 2028. Two of the biggest winners from this trend are Alphabet and Broadcom.

Alphabet developed its TPUs more than a decade ago, and its comprehensive ecosystem is starting to rival Nvidia's. Not only is TPU growth supported by Alphabet's internal use and its cloud offering, but it is also beginning to sell its solutions to external data center operators, such as Anthropic and OpenAI.

Bloomberg Intelligence believes that TPU sales outside of Google Cloud could grow from just $12 billion this year to over $135 billion in 2028. This is a huge revenue driver for both Alphabet and Broadcom, which appear to be two of the biggest winners in this rotation.

It has been revealed that even bigger news for Nvidia competitors, though, is that Anthropic (ANT -8.50%) revealed that its Claude Mythos model demonstrated that it can get models up to speed running on AMD GPUs in just two to three days without any human involvement, dramatically cutting down the six to 12 months it used to take a dozen engineers to get models running on different chips. This greatly narrows Nvidia's CUDA moat and opens the door for both AMD and ASICs to take market share.

The timing is great for AMD, as it recently started shipping its complete Helios systems, which combine its GPUs, CPUs, and networking into one package, to large hyperscaler customers. It's significantly cheaper than Nvidia's end-to-end server racks, opening the door to take more market share if it can show strong performance. The manufacturer's CPUs will also play a key role in Alphabet's latest TPU 8tx AI system.

In a recent development, with CUDA's moat weakening, Alphabet, Broadcom, and AMD, all of which have cheaper offerings, should benefit greatly in the coming years. Meanwhile, Nvidia could face not just a loss of share but also margin compression. This could lead to lower profitability even if it can grow its revenue. That's one of the big reasons I prefer the three stocks Tepper was selling over Nvidia.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

As for the other semiconductor stock that Tepper was buying, Micron, I'd be careful. Memory has historically experienced very big boom-and-bust cycles, and, while this supercycle is certainly different, memory still tends to be a commodity.

Micron is also the most exposed of the significant dynamic random access memory (DRAM) makers to any changes in prices of conventional memory, with it having the smallest share of the high bandwidth memory (HBM) market, which has been the driving force of the industry.

Another area of worry is with NAND, or flash memory. While Micron derives the bulk of its memory from DRAM, NAND has grown to about a quarter of its revenue. Hong Kong-based GF Securities recently issued a note saying it expects this market to become oversupplied as soon as next year. While primarily a DRAM maker, Micron would not be immune to a big price pullback in the NAND market.
