    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Solana (SOL +2.73%) isn't a cryptocurrency focused on providing privacy, but given the new set of features it just released, that could well change, and the result might be sensational for its holders.
    • Sources indicate that those encrypted balances will exist on a blockchain that's already vibrant with applications and tokenized assets, which means Solana could someday support private financial systems if the Rings' features are built out a bit more and the ecosystem takes to using them.
    • Solana's Privacy Rings are shielded pools of tokens, meaning they're shared vaults where balances stay encrypted on the blockchain.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Alex Carchidi – Nov 22, 2026 at 5:27AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Solana ›.

    Solana (SOL +2.73%) isn't a cryptocurrency focused on providing privacy, but given the new set of features it just released, that could well change, and the result might be sensational for its holders. On Nov. 10, the Solana-focused infrastructure tech giant Helius launched a new system called Solana Privacy Rings. The Rings enable users to hold and send Solana tokens with amounts encrypted, making its functionality similar to a subset of the privacy features of dedicated privacy coins like Zcash (ZEC +4.88%).

    Sources indicate that those encrypted balances will exist on a blockchain that's already vibrant with applications and tokenized assets, which means Solana could someday support private financial systems if the Rings' features are built out a bit more and the ecosystem takes to using them. So is this coin worth buying right now with $500, given this news?

    Solana's Privacy Rings are shielded pools of tokens, meaning they're shared vaults where balances stay encrypted on the blockchain.

    Industry observers note that in the default Ring, the asset being held and its amount are private, but the sender and recipient are public. Only customized Rings intended for financial institutions, slated to launch sometime in Q4 of 2026, will add an anonymous mode that masks the senders and recipients of the funds.

    So, while a latest set of privacy features on Solana is a modest plus for holders, and it could get even better over time if they take off, the coin is still not a direct competitor to Zcash or other privacy coins.

    CRYPTO · As of 6:42 AM ET 11/22/26.

    Nor is privacy completely new to Solana.

    Its Confidential Transfers feature, which also hides transaction amounts, was restarted on June 17 after a year offline for security fixes. But in 2025, the Solana Foundation called the feature's usage "extremely low," a reminder that availability doesn't guarantee use. That's not too surprising, as again, Zcash and other privacy coins have more and stronger (and more tested) privacy features anyway, so they are better positioned to capture demand within crypto.

    Recent findings suggest that another wrinkle here is that those other privacy coins tend to lack features Solana has, such as native tokenized assets, smart contract support, and a cheap and speedy network. For the most part, these are what make the fresh Ring feature on Solana interesting, but as of now, the market hasn't sent a strong signal that its differentiating capabilities are actually valuable.

    Solana itself will mostly benefit from the latest privacy features if they encourage more capital to flow to and around its network, which hasn't happened yet.

    Recent findings suggest that for its part, Helius will charge usage credits per private transaction proof its system validates. Solana's holders will gain only from the network fees that each transaction requires, which are fairly minimal on an individual basis. Across the entire chain, Solana collected $353,012 in fees over the 24 hours through Nov. 16. If that pace held for a year, fees would equal about 0.3% of Solana's $41.8 billion market cap.

    The stronger argument for buying Solana here is what the newly introduced privacy capabilities could unlock.

    In a recent development, the chain at the moment hosts $14.1 billion in stablecoins and $5.1 billion in tokenized real-world assets (RWAs). Few businesses would want their payroll data or supplier payments visible to their competitors, and customized Rings that are equipped with auditor access are built for them.

    In a recent development, nonetheless, regulation could blunt that demand, if it even exists within Solana's ecosystem at all. Starting July 1, 2027, the European Union will bar licensed crypto exchanges and custodians from handling privacy coins, and it's unclear if the Rings will mean Solana is classified in that same bucket.

    Industry observers note that as an investor who's bullish on privacy tech and privacy coins, I think Solana's investment thesis is stronger now than before, and I'm optimistic about the expansion of the Rings feature set. But for most investors, the upside here is incremental at best, and so there's no latest reason to buy Solana.

    Tyler Herro scores 50, officials miss late out-of-bounds call on Joel Embiid in 76ers' 132-129 win over Bucks

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (432 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Yahoo

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tyler Herro scored a career-high 50 points Saturday, but that wasn't enough for the Milwaukee Bucks to get their second win of the season in a 132-129 defeat to the Philadelphia 76ers.
    • Milwaukee was deprived of an opportunity to take the lead in the closing seconds when officials missed Joel Embiid stepping out of bounds.
    • Rookie Brayden Burries hit a corner 3-pointer for the Bucks to cut the Sixers' lead to 130-129.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tyler Herro scored a career-high 50 points Saturday, but that wasn't enough for the Milwaukee Bucks to get their second win of the season in a 132-129 defeat to the Philadelphia 76ers.

    Milwaukee was deprived of an opportunity to take the lead in the closing seconds when officials missed Joel Embiid stepping out of bounds.

    Rookie Brayden Burries hit a corner 3-pointer for the Bucks to cut the Sixers' lead to 130-129. After a timeout, LeBron James threw an inbounds pass to Embiid, who attempted to dribble out the clock near the Milwaukee basket. Embiid stepped out of bounds at the baseline with his left foot, but the officials did not call the turnover and Herro was forced to foul.

    The Bucks could not challenge the non-call because they were out of replay challenges.

    Embiid made his two free throws to put Philadelphia ahead by 3, but the Bucks still had 1.5 seconds remaining to try for a tying basket.

    In a recent development, herro received the inbounds pass from Kyle Kuzma at the top of the arc and took one dribble to break free from VJ Edgecombe. Shooting from the right elbow, Herro's 3-pointer went in. However, the shot left his hand after the buzzer.

    The eighth-year guard shot 15 for 23 from the floor, including 7 of 13 on 3-pointers. Herro also hit all 11 of his free throws, adding 11 rebounds and seven assists. Burries finished with 26 points off the bench with 8 rebounds and four assists. Kuzma was the third Bucks player to reach double figures, scoring 12 with five boards.

    Herro's previous career-high was 41 points, reached in a December 2022 win over the Houston Rockets while he was with the Miami Heat.

    Milwaukee lost its 13th consecutive game to drop to 1-16 on the season, the worst mark in the NBA. The Bucks' only win came nearly a month ago on Oct. 26, a 110-102 victory over the Indiana Pacers. Up next for them is the Toronto Raptors (6-10) at home on Monday.

    Embiid led the Sixers with 26 points, nearly registering a triple-double with 17 rebounds and nine assists. James added 21 points with 6 boards, 6 assists and 3 steals. Seven Philadelphia players scored in double figures, with Anfernee Simons getting 18 off the bench and Tyrese Maxey tallying 17 points.

    Industry observers note that the 76ers improved to 14-3 with the win, tying the Los Angeles Lakers for the NBA's top record. Philadelphia has won five consecutive games and next faces the Portland Trail Blazers (10-5) on Monday.

    #108088. Latest Update: XRP Is Back Under $1. Is It Finally a Buy?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (701 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: XRP Is Back Under $1. Is It Finally a Buy?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, XRP (XRP +2.97%) is trading for less than $1 again, down more than 55% during the past year.
    • Sources indicate that A fall like that tends to bring out the bargain hunters, especially if you believe Ripple and its products are on their way to becoming an essential part of international finance.
    • But I think some investors are missing something pretty crucial.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Johnny Rice – Nov 22, 2026 at 5:30AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than XRP ›.

    According to recent reports, XRP (XRP +2.97%) is trading for less than $1 again, down more than 55% during the past year. Meanwhile, the privately held manufacturer behind the token, Ripple, looks as strong as ever. Why?

    Sources indicate that A fall like that tends to bring out the bargain hunters, especially if you believe Ripple and its products are on their way to becoming an essential part of international finance. A token that has lost more than half its value looks like a cheap way to get in on a compelling story.

    But I think some investors are missing something pretty crucial.

    CRYPTO · As of 6:40 AM ET 11/22/26.

    It has been revealed that at its Swell conference last month, the manufacturer said it expects to end 2026 with an annualized product revenue run rate approaching $900 million, roughly triple what it was a year ago. It claims it has partnered with more than 1,700 institutions, corporations, and enterprises that are now using Ripple.

    But investors need to realize that Ripple's success is only loosely connected to XRP's.

    Sources indicate that the case for the token has always been that greater demand for Ripple's products means greater demand for XRP. XRP acts as the bridge asset in a payment, typically across international borders. On one side of a transaction, dollars are swapped for XRP, then swapped for, say, euros on the other side.

    It stands to reason, then, that as more customers use Ripple's payment systems, demand for XRP would increase.

    Unfortunately, that job can now be done by RLUSD (RLUSD +0.00%), Ripple's own stablecoin. RLUSD offers most of the speed and cost benefits without anyone having to hold a volatile token along the way -- even for a few moments. That is attractive for banks and financial institutions who don't want any more volatility than is absolutely necessary.

    Recent findings suggest that while customers can still use either one, Ripple is clearly pushing RLUSD hard. Its website reads: "Integrate stablecoin payments into your business." That doesn't bode well for XRP over time as RLUSD becomes the bridge asset of choice.

    What's more, Ripple still unlocks 1 billion XRP from escrow every month, and while the company relocks 70% to 80% of it, that still leaves 200 million to 300 million upcoming tokens entering circulation each month. There's creates constant pricing pressure from Ripple itself.

    Industry observers note that at present, about 60% of XRP investors hold it at an average cost of $1.44 -- about 50% more than XRP's current price. That will make it hard for XRP to break out, as investors who have been sitting on losses sell whenever the token nears their break-even point.

    Sources indicate that I had expected XRP to be back below $1 by 2031, and obviously it got there a whole lot faster. XRP could certainly go on another run, but with the structural forces the way that they are, I don't see why this would change in the long run.

    Industry observers note that crypto is notoriously hard to value because there are no earnings or cash flows to analyze. There aren't any hard, objective figures to hold on to. Most of crypto seems to be valued based on perception alone, and the expectation that other investors will pay more for it than current holders. And the truth is, XRP has had some serious catalysts in the last two years, and yet it is still back under $1.

    Sources indicate that I think investors have woken up to the fact that Ripple can keep growing rapidly while XRP continues to struggle. That's why I'm going to pass on XRP under $1.

Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said.

    Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

    Sources indicate that additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value.     Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the manufacturer if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he said. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

    Industry observers note that "Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.

    Sources indicate that had an investor parked $500 in Berkshire stock in 1965 and held on until Buffett stepped down, it would have grown into a whopping $24 million. The same investment in an S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) index fund would have grown into just $199,851 over the same period.

    Buffett achieved those returns by focusing on companies with steady growth, reliable profits, and experienced management teams. He never chased the hottest trends, so you wouldn't find him piling money into artificial intelligence (AI) stocks. However, three of Berkshire's top holdings are using AI to supercharge their legacy businesses, and they represent 41.6% of the value of the conglomerate's stock portfolio.

    Warren Buffett. Image source: The Motley Fool.

    Alphabet (GOOG -2.59%)(GOOGL -2.70%) is the parent manufacturer of Google, YouTube, Waymo, and a host of other subsidiaries. It has become a leader in the AI race by integrating it into legacy platforms like Google Search, and by helping businesses tap into the technology via Google Cloud.

Alphabet notes these features are fueling increased Google Search usage, driving the platform's advertising revenue to all-time highs in recent quarters.

    Industry observers note that berkshire initially bought Alphabet stock in the third quarter of 2025, while Buffett was still at the helm, but Abel has increased the position sixfold this year. Berkshire now owns 78.8 million Class A shares and 27.2 million Class C shares worth a combined $29.6 billion.

    It has been revealed that coca-Cola (KO +0.94%) is the world's largest beverage company, but building a portfolio of 200 brands and managing supply chains across more than 200 countries wouldn't be possible without the help of technology.     In 2024, Coca-Cola signed a deal to spend $1.1 billion on the Microsoft (MSFT -2.77%) Azure cloud platform over five years, where it will access tools like the Copilot virtual assistant to support its AI transformation.

    Coca-Cola is one of Berkshire's oldest holdings. Buffett spent approximately $1.3 billion acquiring 400 million shares between 1988 and 1994, and the conglomerate still holds every single one. The position is worth $39.5 billion today, and it will pay Berkshire $848 million in dividends this year alone.

    Apple (AAPL -1.90%) is gunning to become the world's biggest distributor of AI to consumers. It boasts an installed base of more than 2.5 billion active devices around the globe, which mostly include iPhones, iPads, and Mac computers, and it's fitting them with increasingly powerful chips to run the Apple Intelligence suite of AI features and applications.

    According to recent reports, apple Intelligence includes writing tools that can summarize and draft emails or text messages for the user. It can also prioritize notifications based on what each user deems most notable. It even features an upgraded version of the Safari internet browser, which can alert the user to changes to their favorite web pages, so they know immediately if a product they were following is back in stock or is on sale.

    Apple remains one of the most successful investments of Buffett's entire career. He spent approximately $38 billion accumulating shares between 2016 and 2023, and by the beginning of 2024, the position was worth over $170 billion. But it accounted for more than half the value of Berkshire's entire portfolio at that point, so Buffett and his team offloaded 75% of the conglomerate's stake by the end of 2025 to lock in gains and reduce concentration risk.

    Nevertheless, it remains Berkshire's single largest position with a portfolio weighting of 22.4%, so the conglomerate will still do exceptionally well if Apple dominates the consumer AI market.

    #108076. Here's the Average Social Security Benefit at 62 vs. 70

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (783 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    Here's the Average Social Security Benefit at 62 vs. 70

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 22, 2026 at 6:00AM EST.
    • The gap between claiming early and waiting is often viewed through the lens of a single check.
    • In a recent development, over a full year, this monthly difference amounts to $10,203.36 in additional income.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 22, 2026 at 6:00AM EST.

    The gap between claiming early and waiting is often viewed through the lens of a single check. As of December 2025, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA), the average Social Security benefit for someone age 70 is $2,274.68 per month. That's $850.28 more than the $1,424.40 monthly average for those age 62.

    In a recent development, over a full year, this monthly difference amounts to $10,203.36 in additional income. While many workers begin receiving benefits as soon as they reach the earliest eligibility age, the result is a significantly lower baseline for the duration of retirement.

    These averages reflect a snapshot of everyone right now receiving benefits at these specific ages as of December 2025, the most recent data available.

    It has been revealed that these figures don't yet include the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) that will take effect in 2027. That adjustment will add about $51 a month to the age-62 average and about $82 a month to the age-70 average. These raises are supposed to help checks keep pace with inflation, though they don't always do so and can vary widely each year.

    The size of your checks varies in part on your age at sign-up and your full retirement age (FRA). This ranges from 66 to 67, depending on your birth year, and it's 67 for everyone born in 1960 or later. This age serves as the anchor for the permanent reductions applied to early claimers and the credits earned by those who wait.

    It has been revealed that the SSA bases your benefit on your average monthly income during your 35 highest-earning years, which it adjusts for inflation and runs through the primary insurance amount (PIA) formula. Social Security was designed to replace only about 40% of pre-retirement income. This share is well short of what most retirees need, so benefits usually function as supplemental income alongside savings or other sources, regardless of your claiming age.

    Claiming at age 62 locks in a permanent 30% reduction if your FRA is 67. Conversely, waiting past your FRA earns you delayed retirement credits worth 8% a year. This increase totals 24% by age 70. These mechanics create the wide range of averages seen across different age groups.

    Gender differences also play a role in these population averages. At age 62, the average benefit among men is $1,572.83, while the average among women is $1,285.50, a gap of $287.33 per month. By age 70, the gap reaches $505.54 per month, with men averaging $2,529.62 and women averaging $2,024.08.

    Recent findings suggest that longevity also factors into the financial picture for most retirees. At age 65, men are expected to live about 18 more years, and women about 21 more years, according to the SSA. If you live an average lifespan, you tend to receive roughly the same total over your lifetime regardless of when you claim.

    These figures are snapshots of current beneficiaries, not a guarantee of what any one person will receive. While the averages provide a benchmark, your own benefit depends on your unique work history and when you choose to claim.

    Sources indicate that claiming Social Security at 62 can be advantageous if you have a short life expectancy or if you are unable to work and don't have enough personal savings to cover your costs on your own. It might also make sense if you're married and your spouse has earned significantly more than you throughout their career. Claiming early may enable them to delay their own application until they qualify for larger checks.

    Sources indicate that on the other hand, you might prefer to put off your Social Security application until 70 if you have a family history of longevity, are still working well into your 60s, or have enough personal savings that you don't need your checks right now. If you're the higher-earning spouse, delaying your application could increase your future household benefits as well.

    It's also fine to choose a claiming age that's somewhere in the middle, like your FRA. This helps you avoid the early claiming penalty without requiring you to wait until 70 to start receiving checks.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Stefon Walters – Nov 22, 2026 at 6:13AM EST.

    For most American retirees, Social Security plays a large role in their retirement income. In some cases, it's most of their income; in many, it's all of their retirement income. That's why the decision of when to claim shouldn't be glossed over.

    Sources indicate that you can begin claiming benefits at age 62, but your benefit will be reduced, making it a trade-off some aren't willing to take. You can also delay benefits until age 70, which has the opposite effect, but is it worth it?

    Here are three reasons why it is.

    Your full retirement age is when you're qualified to receive your full monthly benefit, called your primary insurance amount (PIA). For anyone born in 1960 or later, full retirement age is presently 67, but you can delay benefits until you turn 70 and receive a bump for each month you delay past 67.

    For each month you delay benefits past your full retirement age, you'll receive Delayed Retirement Credits (DRCs) equal to two-thirds of 1% monthly. This works out to 8% annually, and a 24% total boost if your full retirement age is 67 and you delay until 70.

    In many cases, waiting for the increased monthly benefits results in a higher lifetime payout.

    In a recent development, social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is added as a percentage to someone's current benefits. By delaying benefits until 70 and securing a higher monthly benefit, you also lock in larger dollar raises with each COLA.

    In a recent development, for example, if your PIA is $2,000, next year's 3.6% COLA would raise it to $2,072. However, if you delayed benefits until 70, boosting your benefit to $2,480, a 3.6% COLA would raise it to $2,569.

    That's an extra $204 for the year just from the one COLA, but over time, the larger dollar increases compound.

    Social Security survivor benefits provide benefit support for a surviving spouse after the primary earner passes away.

    Unlike spousal benefits -- which allow the claiming spouse to receive up to 50% of the primary spouse's PIA -- the person receiving survivor benefits receives 100% of the dead spouse's benefit, including any DRCs received.

    Industry observers note that as an example, let's return to someone whose PIA is $2,000, meaning they'd receive $2,480 if they delayed benefits until age 70. If their spouse claims spousal benefits, they could receive up to $1,000 in benefits, even though the primary spouse is receiving more than their PIA. However, if the primary spouse passes away, the surviving spouse could receive the full $2,480.

    Michael Carrick said he had to be careful with Mason Mount after the England midfielder handed Manchester United an injury scare in their friendly draw with Paris St Germain.

    The 27-year-old has been successfully deployed by Carrick in a central midfield role during pre-season, leading to speculation that United may not make another expected signing in that department.

    “He [Mount] got kicked. We just wanted to be careful and look after him,” Carrick, the United head coach, told reporters in Sweden.

    “We’ve been lucky with injuries so far, so we wanted to be careful.”.

    Breaking: 3 Retirement Expenses You May Not Be Prepared For -- But Need to Be

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Retirement is often portrayed as a time when you finally get to enjoy the money you've spent decades saving.
    • According to recent reports, but the expenses you don't see coming could easily derail your retirement looks and deplete your savings sooner than expected.
    • Many people are able to pay off their mortgages ahead of retirement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Maurie Backman – Nov 22, 2026 at 6:18AM EST.

    Retirement is often portrayed as a time when you finally get to enjoy the money you've spent decades saving. You may have looks to travel, spend more time with family, pursue hobbies, or simply enjoy a slower pace of life.

    According to recent reports, but the expenses you don't see coming could easily derail your retirement looks and deplete your savings sooner than expected. Here are three significant retirement expenses you need to prepare for in advance so you aren't thrown for a loop.

    Many people are able to pay off their mortgages ahead of retirement. But don't assume that your housing costs will be negligible just because you're mortgage-free. Your home will continue to require maintenance. And as it ages, you might need to sink more money into repairs that can be surprisingly expensive.

    There's also the possibility that you may eventually need to modify your home to make it safer and more accessible as you age. Installing grab bars, adding better lighting, or creating wider doorways to accommodate a walker could all require additional spending.

    In a recent development, to avoid a shock, maintain a cash emergency fund outside of your IRA or 401(k), which may be more heavily invested in stocks and other assets whose value can fluctuate. Home repairs in particular are often things that can't wait, so having cash on hand to cover them is key. You may also want to maintain a separate account for eventual renovations if your goal is to age in place.

    Once you retire, you may have more time to spend money on hobbies, travel, dining out, and social activities. Some of these expenses, like newly introduced subscriptions, might seem relatively small individually, but they can add up over time. And if you want to travel a lot, that's something your budget will need to accommodate.

    It's important to create a realistic entertainment budget that reflects the retirement lifestyle you actually want. If you're looking to go overseas three times a year, work that into your financial initiative instead of winging it on the spot.

    You may also want to take some strategic steps to make your desired lifestyle possible. Working an extra year or two to boost savings could help, as could delaying your Social Security benefits for larger monthly checks.

    According to recent reports, you might assume that Medicare will cover most of your healthcare needs as you get older. But Medicare generally doesn't cover ongoing custodial care, such as assistance with bathing, dressing, eating, and other everyday activities. That means you could be responsible for a substantial portion of the cost, if not all of it, if you eventually need in-home assistance, assisted living, or nursing home care.

    In a recent development, the latest CareScout 2025 Cost of Care Survey highlights just how expensive these services have become. Here are the median costs of various types of care on a national level:.

    Because these figures represent national medians, it's important to recognize that costs in your area could be considerably higher. So don't wait until you need long-term care to start thinking about how you'll pay for it.

    Research long-term-care insurance, hybrid life insurance policies with long-term-care benefits, and other potential funding options. Also think about what type of care you'd prefer as you get older and whether your retirement savings can support those expenses.

    In a recent development, ultimately, retirement planning isn't just about having enough money to stop working. It's about having enough money to handle the unexpected while still enjoying the lifestyle you've worked so hard to achieve. Preparing for these three expenses in advance could help prevent unwanted financial stress later.

    • Recent findings suggest that our proprietary Hidden Gems scoring system assigns Slide Insurance Holdings an overall Superscore of 90 out of 100, placing it in the Exceptional category.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Sarah Sidlow – Updated Nov 22, 2026 at 6:27AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Slide Insurance ›.

    In a recent development, when a hurricane tears through a coastal community, the insurance companies that wrote the policies often find themselves in the eye of the financial storm. Slide Insurance Holdings (SLDE -2.38%) has spent the last five years betting it can do better than the incumbents that retreated from those markets. Founded in 2021 in Tampa, Florida, the tech giant uses a proprietary platform called Violet to parse massive data sets of property information and risk, essentially cherry-picking the policies that legacy insurers were too afraid or too slow to price correctly. As of Nov. 19, 2026, the stock trades at $26.92, marking a 70% climb over the last 12 months, reflecting a rapid transition from a start-up to a profitable, technology-driven powerhouse.

    Recent findings suggest that our proprietary Hidden Gems scoring system assigns Slide Insurance Holdings an overall Superscore of 90 out of 100, placing it in the Exceptional category. The Superscore is an AI-powered score that evaluates a tech giant's overall strength by combining financial performance, product market position, technological capabilities, leadership quality, and relative valuation. It represents the unification of all our scores into a single score for public companies, with five rating bands: Exceptional (90-100), Strong (75-89), Above Average (60-74), Average (40-59), and Cautious (0-39). A 90 score places the company in the Top ~1% of all companies we score, ahead of roughly 99 out of every 100 firms in our database. This score is a data-driven signal to help you structure your own due diligence, and this article examines both the operational strengths and the structural risks to give you a full picture before you dive deeper.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Slide is a highly capital-efficient business, earning significant profit on a relatively small base of tangible assets. This efficiency means it can turn each point of revenue growth into outsize returns, which helps explain why the market may accept its valuation even amid the volatility typical of property insurance.

    This stock warrants a closer look if...

    You may want to keep researching before buying if...

    The Superscore is one data-driven signal to help you structure your own due diligence, but it should not be treated as a stand-alone buy recommendation. Please weigh this score and our analysis against your own research, financial goals, and personal risk tolerance before making any investment decisions.

    Insurance analysts estimate modest room for growth in the catastrophe insurance field, with exposure growth around 7% annually and reconstruction costs around 5% annually, according to Verisk. And it isn't just single-year weather patterns; expanding footprints in high-hazard zones mean increased opportunities for catastrophe insurance claims.

    Slide hasn't been in business for long, and it built its initial portfolio in large part on policy take-outs from state insurers, meaning it gained thousands of policyholders and millions of premium dollars without significant acquisition costs. That's a lean way to build a business, but the risk is that Slide hasn't proven it can grow organically. That said, Swiss Re says a substantial share of economic catastrophe damage remains uninsured, possibly indicating more market opportunity ahead for Slide.

    The catastrophe insurance industry can be highly volatile, with infrequent events leading to massive losses. Slide has already contended with a few major events since its founding: the 2024 hurricanes Debby, Helene, and Milton, in which it incurred $32.1 million in net catastrophe losses; and connective storms in Florida this year, which led to a $34.1 million loss; neither of those stressed its balance sheet. As it expands in Florida, Texas, and Rhode Island, it has increased its 2026-2027 catastrophe reinsurance program to $5.463 billion in protection. The company's rapid revenue growth and solid combined ratio indicate it has figured out how to thrive profitably in its niche, but more substantial tests are likely ahead for this insurer.

    #108064. The Stock Market Is Doing Something for Only the 5th Time This Century, and History States It's Obvious What Comes Next for Stocks

    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    The Stock Market Is Doing Something for Only the 5th Time This Century, and History States It's Obvious What Comes Next for Stocks

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that with less than six weeks left in 2026, investors have little to complain about.
    • Sources indicate that while Wall Street's major stock indexes have made a habit of climbing the proverbial wall of worry and rising over the long term, history also makes clear that bull markets don't last forever.
    • It has been revealed that though any number of headwinds can knock the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite off their respective pedestals, one stands out.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Sean Williams – Nov 22, 2026 at 6:36AM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›.

    Industry observers note that with less than six weeks left in 2026, investors have little to complain about. The mature-stock-driven Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -1.93%), broad-based S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%), and tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.28%) have all catapulted to several record highs this year, driven by the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out, better-than-expected corporate earnings, and initial public offering euphoria.

    Sources indicate that while Wall Street's major stock indexes have made a habit of climbing the proverbial wall of worry and rising over the long term, history also makes clear that bull markets don't last forever. If things seem too perfect for investors, they often are.

    It has been revealed that though any number of headwinds can knock the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite off their respective pedestals, one stands out. We're currently witnessing the stock market do something for only the fifth time this century, and history doesn't mince its words about what comes next for stocks.

    Despite a parabolic move in outstanding margin debt sending all the wrong signals, the biggest worry for Wall Street and investors is premium stock valuations.

    To be clear, past events can't guarantee what the future holds. Nevertheless, history has shown a tendency to rhyme on Wall Street more often than not, making it an excellent teaching tool for those investors willing to listen.

    Most investors rely on the time-tested price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio when evaluating individual companies or the broader market. While the P/E ratio, which is derived using trailing 12-month earnings per share (EPS), is incredibly useful for promptly sizing up mature businesses, it can lose its utility entirely when recessions occur and EPS turns negative.

    Industry observers note that for Wall Street's broad-market stock indexes, the S&P 500's Shiller P/E Ratio, also known as the Cyclically Adjusted P/E Ratio (CAPE Ratio), is a far superior valuation tool. The Shiller P/E is based on average inflation-adjusted EPS over the trailing 10 years, meaning recessions won't render it useless.

    Sources indicate that though economists introduced the S&P 500's Shiller P/E Ratio less than four decades ago, it's been backtested to January 1871. Over these 156 years, the average reading is a relatively modest 17.45. As of the closing bell on Nov. 17, it was 38.76, or 122% above this long-term average.

    Stock Market Shiller PE Ratio on the verge of taking out its Dot Com Bubble all-time high 🚨 🤯 👀 https://t.co/CtCmSgWnLt.

    What's particularly interesting is how the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite have behaved once the CAPE Ratio surpasses 30, which has happened six times since January 1871, and five times this century, including the present:.

    On the one hand, the S&P 500's Shiller P/E can't pinpoint when the major stock indexes will peak or which catalyst(s) will send stocks tumbling. But this arbitrary line in the sand has an impeccable track record of foreshadowing significant downturns (20% or greater) in the stock market's major indexes.

    History makes it crystal clear that premium valuations aren't sustainable on Wall Street.

    Sometimes, history doesn't offer the most glowing forecast for the stock market. But altering your perspective can vastly change the projected outcome.

    To state what can be an unpleasant truth, stock market corrections, bear markets, and even occasional crashes are normal and healthy events. Given that most of these events are driven by investor emotions, there's not much that can be done from a fiscal or monetary policy perspective to prevent them. Consider these events the cost of admission to take part in one of the world's greatest wealth creators.

    But stock market corrections, bear markets, and crashes share an notable trait: they're historically short-lived.

    The analysts at Bespoke Investment Group examined every S&P 500 bull and bear market since the start of the Great Depression in September 1929, finding a sizable gap between optimism and pessimism on Wall Street.

    According to Bespoke's data set, released in late May, the average S&P 500 bear market finds its trough in 286 calendar days (about 9.5 months), while the typical bull market persists for 1,023 calendar days, or nearly 3.6 times as long.

    In a recent development, the analysts at Crestmont Research took things even further by examining the rolling 20-year total returns of the benchmark S&P 500 since 1900. Since the S&P wasn't incepted until 1923, this meant tracking the total return of its components in other major indexes back to 1900.

    Crestmont's data yielded 107 separate rolling 20-year periods (1900-1919, 1901-1920, and so on, through 2006-2025), all of which generated a positive average annual return.

    Industry observers note that hypothetically speaking, since S&P 500-tracking funds didn't exist on U.S. exchanges until January 1993, if an investor had purchased an S&P 500 index fund at any point between 1900 and 2006 and simply held it for 20 years, they would have generated a profit every single time, including dividends. It didn't matter if they bought near a top, before a recession, depression, war, pandemic, or high inflation... the result was always the same.

    Even when the stock market gives investors lemons, history indicates make some lemonade and be patient.
